claims.text: The alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The proposed initial material is a polycrystalline alloy produced by arc melting and subsequent homogenization.
The processed WTaTiVZr alloy has a uniform solid-solution microstructure.
WTaTiVZr may exhibit nanoscale chemical segregation at grain boundaries.
The atomic-size mismatch among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces local lattice strains and a chemically complex environment.
Ti and Zr tend to segregate to grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
Local lattice distortions lower the critical stresses needed to activate multiple slip systems.
Local lattice distortion activates additional or non-conventional slip systems in WTaTiVZr.
The lattice-distortion effects enhance dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr at service temperatures.
Solute segregation modifies grain-boundary energy and embrittlement behavior.
Ti- and Zr-associated grain-boundary modification increases grain-boundary cohesion.
Enhanced dislocation mobility and increased grain-boundary cohesion delay crack nucleation.
Enhanced dislocation mobility and increased grain-boundary cohesion retard crack propagation.
The combined lattice-distortion and grain-boundary effects give WTaTiVZr greater plastic deformation capacity than pure tungsten.
The combined lattice-distortion and grain-boundary effects give WTaTiVZr greater toughness than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten lacks the proposed microstructural benefits and is more prone to brittle fracture under high thermal loads.
Under otherwise identical testing, WTaTiVZr should have higher plastic strain to failure than commercially pure tungsten.
Under otherwise identical testing, WTaTiVZr should have higher fracture toughness or energy absorption than commercially pure tungsten.
The predicted performance enhancement should occur between approximately 800 and 1200 °C, where dislocation activity is prominent.
The hypothesis may cease to hold at ambient temperature or under extreme irradiation if irradiation changes microstructural stability or promotes phase transformations.
